old: so long as I had stayed at home
new: if only I had stayed at home
reason: "so long as" normally signals a condition ("provided that"), but here it's used to mean "if only" — a listener's first parse (I'd rather have a third of my wealth, provided I'd stayed home) inverts the intended sense (I wish I'd stayed home instead of gaining this wealth) and forces a re-read.

new: Memnon, son of the Dawn goddess
reason: Antilochus's killer is named only by a periphrasis a first-time listener has no way to decode; the sentence tells us someone specific killed him but withholds who, which reads as a dropped antecedent rather than a deliberate epithet.

old: Halosydne’s chickens, as they call them
new: the sea goddess's brood, as sailors call them
reason: "Halosydne" is never introduced elsewhere in the book, so the aside names an unfamiliar figure and calls seals her "chickens" with no context for the joke/epithet, which stalls a listener mid-sentence.

old: even though Orestes has been beforehand with you in killing him
new: even though Orestes has beaten you to killing him
reason: "Been beforehand with you" meaning "gotten there before you did" is a period construction that a modern ear is likely to mishear or fail to parse on first listen.

old: bound the oars to the thole pins with twisted thongs of leather
new: lashed the oars to the oarlocks with twisted leather thongs
reason: "Thole pins" is obscure nautical vocabulary a general listener won't recognize; the action (securing oars for rowing) is clear enough from context but the specific term adds unnecessary friction.

old: the hole through which the thong went for pulling the door to
new: the hole where the latch-thong ran, used to pull the door shut
reason: "Pulling the door to" (archaic adverbial "to" meaning "closed") reads as an incomplete sentence to modern ears expecting "to [something]"; combined with unexplained door-latch mechanics, it's an awkward stumble for a listener.
